newsitem.title: USA: Judge threatens sanctions in O.J. Simpson trial.
newsitem.headline: Judge threatens sanctions in O.J. Simpson trial.

text.p: The judge in the O.J. Simpson civil trial threatened "draconian" sanctions Friday against the father of murder victim Ronald Goldman because of comments he made that may have violated the court's gag-order.
"If parties are going to violate these orders, I don't think monetary sanctions are going to be sufficient," Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki told laywers for both sides.
"It is my intention to seek an appropriate remedy for the situation which I think will be somewhat draconian, and that's not an understatement," he said.

The judge's anger was prompted by one of Simpson's lawyers, Robert Blasier, who complained about comments Fred Goldman made on CNN on Thursday night and also about an impromptu news conference Goldman held outside the courthouse during the Friday lunch recess.
Fujisaki, a no-nonsense jurist who has already barred TV cameras from the civil trial, last month issued a gag-order preventing lawyers and parties in the case from commenting about it publicly.

Goldman, whose son was murdered June 12, 1994 along with Simpson's ex-wife Nicole Brown, is one of the plaintiffs in the wrongful-death civil suit filed against the ex-football star and movie actor. Simpson was acquitted last year of criminal murder charges.

Goldman, who was very outspoken during the criminal trial, called in to CNN's Larry King Live show Thursday night to defend his dead son's honour after another caller suggested the younger Goldman's lifestyle may have contributed to his death.
In court Friday, Goldman's attorney defended his client's action, saying it came after someone "trashed my client's murdered son.
"My client called in to express his outrage," Daniel Petrocelli said. "I strongly object to my client being accused of violating the order without any proof."
Fujisaki turned to the attorney and said: "If your client can't heed the court's orders, we're going to have a problem.
"I'm sorry your client is not here so I could personally admonish him."
Goldman had been in the courtroom for the morning session, but was absent in the afternoon after giving his news conference to refute allegations that his legal defence fund was misusing donations.

As it was, Fujisaki did not impose any sanctions, although TV legal expert Roger Cossack, who was outside the courtroom said he believed the judge had the power to impose a jail term for contempt of court.

The legal tiff interrupted another ponderous day of questioning of potential jurors. After a week, Fujisaki has so far approved only 46 potential jurors for the pool from which 12 jurors and eight alternates will ultimately be selected.
Of those so far selected, 21 are white, 20 are black and five are from other ethnic groups.
Most of the prospective panellists interviewed have divided along racial lines, with whites generally believing Simpson, who is black, was guilty of killing his white ex-wife and Ronald Goldman.
Generally, blacks support the innocent verdict and often express belief in a police conspiracy theory advanced by defence attorneys in last year's criminal trial.

For the third day in a row, Simpson was not present in the courthouse where he is being sued by the families of the murder victims. If he is found responsible for the wrongful deaths of Nicole Brown and Ronald Goldman, he could be forced to pay millions of dollars in damages.
In his comments to reporters, Fred Goldman denied allegations of fraud leveled at his "Ron Goldman Justice Fund".
Goldman said "every penny," except for the costs of sending out letters asking for donations, went toward the fund to help pay lawyers' fees.
He said the fund had received "hundreds of thousands" of dollars in contributions, but that they could not hope to cover the estimated multimillion-dollar costs of the civil case.
